title: Trump says he will appoint a new AI adviser, without providing details
author: Daniel Nenni
text:
Daniel Nenni
Founder
Staff member

President Donald Trump said he plans to appoint an artificial-intelligence adviser and create an “AI force,” but offered no details about the position’s authority, membership, timetable or policy agenda.

The announcement, made on Truth Social, would give the administration a second official commonly described as an “AI czar.” Venture capitalist David Sacks held that role before stepping down earlier this year; Reuters reported that he continues advising Trump from outside government.

Trump has argued that the United States should accelerate AI development and avoid rules that could slow innovation. He has suggested that law can address harmful uses of the technology, a view aligned with Sacks’ preference for placing responsibility on developers without extensive federal oversight.

The announcement arrives as Washington wrestles with questions about advanced AI: who should test models, when companies must disclose risks, how copyright and privacy rules apply, and whether federal policy should override a patchwork of state laws. It also comes amid competition with China, with AI security expected to feature in U.S.-China discussions.

Why it matters
A presidential AI adviser can shape far more than technology policy. The role could influence national security, export controls, government procurement, energy and data-center construction, workforce policy, research funding and rules faced by AI companies. An “AI force” could also coordinate agencies that otherwise approach these issues separately.

But titles alone reveal little. The adviser’s identity, legal mandate, access to Trump, staffing and relationship with cabinet agencies will determine whether the office becomes a center of power or a political signal. Trump’s lack of specifics creates uncertainty for companies, regulators and safety advocates.

The central question is whether the initiative will produce coherent governance while preserving innovation—or primarily accelerate deployment while leaving oversight fragmented. Until the administration names its adviser and defines the force, its significance remains unresolved. (Reuters)
